title: Cookies, and what they cannot prove

terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. run.js starts the cupboard server, runs your functions against it and prints every request and answer.

tasks.title: Sign in and bring the cookies back
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/cookies.js`, make `playlistAs(base, presenter, key)` sign in to the server at `base`, then ask for the playlist as the presenter who signed in:

1. a `POST` to `/studio/sign-in` whose body is JSON with `presenter` and `key`, and nothing else
2. when the server refuses the sign-in, with a status that is not in the 200s, it throws an `Error` and asks for nothing more
3. otherwise a `GET` for `/studio/playlist` that carries every cookie the sign-in answer set, as `name=value` pairs in one `cookie` header

It gives back the body of the playlist answer.

Check starts a server of its own that sets one cookie, or several with dates and `=` signs in them, and answers with the playlist only when its cookies come back exactly. It looks at both requests its server received.
nextSteps: Send the sign-in the way Part 2 sent JSON.
Read every set-cookie line of its answer, one by one.
Keep only the name=value part of each line, and join them for one cookie header.
Run `node run.js`: the studio app's playlist request today gets 401, yours should not.
hints: `fetch` keeps no cookies, unlike a browser. Whatever the sign-in sets, your code has to send back itself.

`response.headers.getSetCookie()` gives a list with one text per set-cookie line. `headers.get('set-cookie')` joins them with commas, and an `Expires` date has a comma of its own. In each line, everything before the first semicolon is `name=value`; the rest are attributes for the browser, never sent back.

`const pairs = signIn.headers.getSetCookie().map((line) => line.split(';')[0].trim())`, then `fetch(new URL('/studio/playlist', base), { headers: { cookie: pairs.join('; ') } })`, and `return` its `text()`.

tasks.title: Choose the cookies a request carries
tasks.description:
A browser does this part for you. Under `// Task 2`, make `cookieHeader(jar, address, now)` do it the way a browser does. `jar` is a list of the cookies a browser keeps, each one:

`{ name, value, domain, hostOnly, path, secure, httpOnly, expires }`

`hostOnly` is `true` for a cookie set without a `Domain` attribute, and `expires` is a time in milliseconds, or `null` for a cookie that lasts until the browser closes.

It gives back the text of the `cookie` header that a request for `address` carries at the time `now`: `name=value` for every cookie whose host, path, `Secure` and expiry rules from the lesson allow it, separated by a semicolon and a space, in any order. When no cookie goes, it gives back `''`.

Check calls `cookieHeader` with a jar and times of its own, and addresses on other hosts, paths, schemes and ports.
nextSteps: Take the address apart with `new URL`, as in the first issue.
Go through the jar and keep each cookie only when its host, its path, Secure and its expiry all allow it.
Write the ones you kept as name=value, joined by a semicolon and a space.
Run `node run.js`: of the four addresses, only the first carries the session cookie.
hints: Four questions per cookie, each a yes or a no: the host, the path, Secure, and whether it has expired. Two things never matter for requests: the port, and HttpOnly.

A host is under a domain only when it ends with a dot and the domain. A path is under the cookie's path when it is the same, or starts with it and the next character is a slash, or the cookie's path ends with one. `expires` is either `null` or a time to compare with `now`.

`jar.filter((c) => hostOk && pathOk && (!c.secure || url.protocol === 'https:') && (c.expires === null || c.expires > now))`, where `hostOk` is `c.hostOnly ? host === c.domain : host === c.domain || host.endsWith('.' + c.domain)`, then `` .map((c) => `${c.name}=${c.value}`).join('; ') ``.

docs.title: Using HTTP cookies: where cookies are sent

tasks.title: Write the cookie that keeps a presenter signed in
tasks.description:
Now the server's side. Under `// Task 3`, make `sessionCookie(id, path, seconds)` give back the text of the `set-cookie` header the cupboard server sends after a sign-in, without the header's name. It sets a cookie called `session` whose value is `id`, and its attributes say that it is:

- sent back only to the host that set it, never to other hosts under its domain
- sent only with requests for `path` and the paths under it
- kept for `seconds` seconds
- sent only over https
- never readable by a page's scripts
- left off requests that pages on other sites make, such as forms they post, but still sent when someone follows a link to the station

Check calls `sessionCookie` with ids, paths and lifetimes of its own, and reads the attributes in any order and letter case.
nextSteps: Start with the cookie itself: its name, an equals sign and the id.
Add one attribute per line of the task, each after a semicolon and a space.
Pick each attribute from the lesson's list, and leave out the one that would widen where the cookie goes.
Run `node run.js` and read the Task 3 line.
hints: Every line of the task is one attribute, except the first: a cookie goes back only to the host that set it when it has no `Domain` at all.
`Path` takes the path and `Max-Age` the seconds. `Secure` and `HttpOnly` take no value. `SameSite` has three values, and the one the task describes lets links from other sites through.
`` return `session=${id}; Path=${path}; Max-Age=${seconds}; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax` ``.

tasks.title: Find who is signed in, from the session only
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, make `whoIsThis(cookie, sessions, now)` take the text of a request's `cookie` header, or `null` when the request had none (its cookies are separated by semicolons, with or without a space after each), the sessions the server keeps, an object from session id to `{ presenter, expires }`, and a time `now` in milliseconds.

It gives back the `presenter` of the session named by the request's cookie called `session`, or `null` when there is no such cookie, the server keeps no session with that id, or the session's `expires` is not later than `now`. Any other cookie, like one called `presenter`, proves nothing.

Check calls `whoIsThis` with cookie headers, sessions and times of its own: some with a presenter cookie that names someone else, some with ids the server never made.
nextSteps: Handle a request with no cookie header first.
Split the header into its cookies, and each cookie at its first `=` only.
Find the cookie called exactly session, and look its value up in sessions.
Check that the session has not expired, then run `node run.js`.
hints: The browser sends whatever cookies it holds, and a person can change any of them. Only an id the server made and stored itself tells you who someone is.

Cookies in the header are separated by semicolons, with or without a space. `indexOf('=')` finds the first `=`, and an id may have more `=` signs in it. `sessions[id]` is `undefined` for an id the server never made.

Loop over `(cookie ?? '').split(';')`, and for the part whose name, `part.slice(0, at).trim()`, is `'session'`, take `sessions[part.slice(at + 1).trim()]`. Return its `presenter` when it exists and `expires > now`, and `null` at the end.
